title: Before sleep
hookLine: a traditional Jewish bedtime prayer begins by forgiving anyone who hurt you that day

cards: What does the mind do in the last minutes before sleep? Lights off, phone down, and the day starts replaying. The comment in the meeting.
The text that was a little too short. The friend who didn't ask how it went. Small things, mostly.
But small things left overnight have a way of being bigger by morning, and bigger still by the end of the week. A Jewish tradition has an answer built into bedtime itself.
Before the Shema is said at night, a prayer comes first, and it opens with forgiveness.

teach.b: First, where it sits. The bedtime Shema is a set of prayers said at night, at home, often in bed. In the traditional prayer book, before the Shema itself, there's a short passage addressed to the Master of the world.
In paraphrase: I hereby forgive anyone who angered me or wronged me, whether against my body, my property or my honor, by accident or on purpose, in word or in deed.
It doesn't ask who deserves it, and it isn't limited to today. It covers the whole list in one sweep. Third, the line that surprises people.

teach.h: LET NO ONE BE PUNISHED FOR ME.
teach.b: The prayer goes further: it asks that no one be punished on my account. Not just I let it go, but I don't want them to suffer because of what they did to me.
That's a big request to make about someone who was rude to you at lunch, and it's said at night, while the day's grudges are still fresh. Fourth, a neighbor.

teach.h: NOT THE SUN ON YOUR WRATH.
teach.b: Christians read a line from the letter to the Ephesians that points at the same hour: "Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath."

Two traditions, each in its own words, both asking that the day's anger be set down at the edge of night. Clear the small debts daily, the way you'd wash the dishes before bed, so you don't wake up to a sink full of them.

how: Jews who say the bedtime Shema (Kriat Shema al ha-Mitah) begin, in the traditional prayer book, with a passage forgiving anyone who wronged them, before saying the Shema.

o: the quiet hour when the day's work must be finished
a rule against going to bed while still angry at a spouse
the day's last minutes, when a bedtime prayer forgives first

games.why: the prayer forgives by accident or on purpose, in word or deed, and asks that no one be punished on my account.

practice: Whatever the hour, sit as if it were the end of the day, and flip back through today, or yesterday if it's morning, like photos.
At each small sting, a word, a look, a silence, don't argue the case; just say silently, I forgive today, and move to the next.
If something is too big for tonight, set it aside, and if you pray, you can use a bedtime prayer from your own tradition.

wordCard.voice: Before sleep. The last minutes of the day, when a Jewish bedtime prayer forgives the day's wrongs before the Shema is said. Today's word.
